messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 38

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rodrigo is a 62-year-old Cuban American man who has spent the better part of four decades as a professional dancer and dance instructor in Miami. He came to the intake appointment moving carefully, as though the body that had once been his instrument now required constant negotiation. He is married, soft-spoken, and chose his words with the deliberateness of someone who has learned that certain words open doors he would rather keep closed.

Fourteen months ago, Rodrigo was driving home from a late evening rehearsal when a pickup truck ran a red light at highway speed and struck the driver's side of his sedan. The impact spun the car across two lanes before it came to rest against a concrete median barrier. What he remembers — and what he cannot entirely remember — is the shriek of metal compressing around him, a sound so absolute it seemed to replace all other sound in the world, and then the horn, his own car's horn, blaring without interruption in the silence that followed. He was conscious throughout. He was alone. It took emergency responders nearly twenty minutes to reach him, and he spent those twenty minutes unable to move, listening to the horn and to what he later described only as "other sounds" he cannot name even now. When he tries to put the event into a coherent account, the narrative fractures. He can describe before and after but the center of it resists language entirely, surfacing instead as a sudden auditory intrusion — the grinding of metal, the horn — that arrives without warning in the middle of a conversation, a lesson, a meal.

In the weeks after the accident, Rodrigo returned to teaching because the studio was what he knew and because stillness felt dangerous. But the studio brought its own difficulties. Students would approach him from behind to correct their posture or offer a steadying hand, and the unexpected contact would send a jolt of alarm through him so sharp that he once stumbled backward into a mirror. He began positioning himself at the edge of every room, facing the door, locating the exits before he located anything else. He told himself this was practical. He had come to believe, with a quiet but immovable certainty, that he had no real capacity to prevent harm from reaching him — that the accident had confirmed something true about his life rather than interrupted it. The shame attached to this belief was not abstract. When the memories came, they brought with them a wave of humiliation he could not fully explain, a sense that what had happened to him was a verdict.

He began staying up past two or three in the morning, moving through the house in the dark, telling himself he was not tired. Sleep felt like a threshold he did not trust himself to cross. On nights when exhaustion overtook him, he would sometimes find himself deliberately trying to go elsewhere in his mind — to empty himself out before the images could arrive. He worked hard, in waking hours, to keep the event at the edge of his thoughts, and when it pressed forward he pushed back, though the effort left him hollowed out by midday. His wife, Marisol, noticed that he had become unreachable in a way she could not name. He was present at the dinner table but not present. She stopped asking about the accident because asking seemed to cost him something visible. The distance between them grew in the way that distances grow when neither person acknowledges them — gradually, and then all at once.

What finally brought Rodrigo to seek help was a moment in class three weeks ago when a student played a recording through a small Bluetooth speaker and the feedback squeal from the device — sharp, sustained, electronic — sent him to the floor with his hands over his ears. His students stood frozen. He sat on the studio floor and understood, perhaps for the first time, that he could not manage this alone. He arrived at the intake hoping, he said, to feel like himself again — though he confessed, almost in the same breath, that he was no longer certain such a self still existed.
